prompt: `/usr/bin/sleep` is on the disk and three people are running `sleep 60` right now. How many of each is there?
hint: One of these lives on the disk and does not change when it runs.

choices.text: Three files and three processes
choices.why: Running a program does not copy it; the file on the disk is untouched.

choices.text: One file and one process
choices.why: They would interfere with each other's memory, which is the thing a process is designed to prevent.

choices.text: One file and three processes
choices.why: Right — the file is unchanged and each run is a separate process with its own memory.

choices.text: Three files and one process
choices.why: Nothing writes extra copies of a binary to run it.

prompt: You write down a PID, wait ten minutes, then `kill` it. What is the risk?
hint: The kernel hands numbers out in order and then starts again.

choices.text: The number will have grown
choices.why: PIDs are not offsets; an old number stays valid until the kernel wraps round to it again.

choices.text: The number belongs to something else
choices.why: Right — PIDs are reused after the counter wraps, so a saved one goes stale.

choices.text: Ten minutes is too long
choices.why: Nothing expires a PID; it is valid for exactly as long as the process lives.

choices.text: The PID is renumbered on a state change
choices.why: A process keeps its number from `fork` to `exit`, whatever it does in between.

prompt: `ps aux` shows a row with `[kthreadd]` in square brackets and zeros in the VSZ and RSS columns. What is it?
hint: The brackets are `ps` saying there is nothing to print.

choices.text: Kernel code with a PID and no memory
choices.why: Right — the brackets mean there is no command line, and the zeros mean no user-space memory.

choices.text: A command line too long to show
choices.why: `ps` truncates long lines instead, and it does not add brackets when it does.

choices.text: A process that exited and awaits collection
choices.why: That one is marked `<defunct>` and shows a `Z` in the state column.

choices.text: A thread of another process
choices.why: Threads need `-L` or `-H`, and they carry their parent's memory figures rather than zeros.

prompt: Expand this to your own shell's process number, in one word: `ps -p ____ -o pid,ppid`
hint: Two characters, and the shell substitutes it before `ps` ever sees it.

prompt: Match each `/proc/PID` entry to what reading it tells you.
hint: All four are files, and each answers a different question about one process.

pairs.right: the arguments it was started with
which binary it is running
the directory it treats as here
the numbered files it has open

right_distractors: how much processor it has used

prompt: Put the steps of running `ls` from a shell in order.
items: bash calls fork, and there are two bashes
the child calls exec and becomes /usr/bin/ls
ls prints and exits with a status
bash's wait returns, sets $?, and prints a prompt
trap: Copy first, replace second; the parent only waits once the child exists.

prompt: Why are `fork` and `exec` two calls rather than one?
hint: Think about what has to happen to the copy before the new program starts.

choices.text: So that a process can be copied without running anything new
choices.why: That happens, but a copy nobody ever `exec`s is the unusual case rather than the reason.

choices.text: Because copying memory is slow and is done in the background
choices.why: `fork` does not copy memory eagerly at all; pages are shared until one side writes.

choices.text: Because the kernel has to schedule the child before it can load a program
choices.why: The child is schedulable immediately, and loading a program does not wait on the scheduler.

choices.text: So the child can change identity, directory and open files in between
choices.why: Right — redirections and a unit file's `User=` both happen in that gap.

prompt: A script does `cd /tmp` and finishes. Your shell's directory is unchanged. Why?
hint: The script ran somewhere, and it was not in your shell.

choices.text: The script's `cd` was undone when it exited from there
choices.why: Nothing undoes it; there is simply no shared directory to undo.

choices.text: The script is a separate process with its own copy
choices.why: Right — which is why `cd` has to be a shell builtin to be useful at all.

choices.text: `cd` inside a script needs `export` to reach the parent
choices.why: `export` passes variables down to children; nothing passes a directory back up.

choices.text: The shell puts its directory back once the command has finished
choices.why: It does not; a builtin `cd` you type yourself changes it and it stays changed.

prompt: A parent collects its child's exit status by calling ____ — the other half of `exit`.
hint: Four letters, and bash has a builtin with the same name.

prompt: `ps -eo stat --no-headers | sort | uniq -c` on a healthy machine gives 36 `S`, 24 `I<` and 1 `R`. What does that say?
hint: Count how many are actually doing something.

choices.text: The machine is starved by one process
choices.why: A single `R` is one process on the run queue, which is the opposite of contention.

choices.text: Something is wrong: just one process started
choices.why: All eighty-five have started; eighty-four of them are waiting for something.

choices.text: It is idle and normal — almost everything is asleep
choices.why: Right, and the `I<` rows are kernel workers doing nothing, which is their job.

choices.text: The kernel threads are blocked
choices.why: `I` is the idle state for a kernel thread; `D` would be the blocked one.

prompt: A process has been in `D` for four minutes. What do you do about it?
hint: Work out first whether a signal would reach it at all.

choices.text: Send it `TERM`, then `KILL`
choices.why: Neither arrives: a signal is delivered on the way back to user space, and it has not come back.

choices.text: `renice` it to 19 so it stops competing
choices.why: Niceness is processor time, and this process is not asking for any.

choices.text: Leave it — `D` is ordinary
choices.why: An instant is ordinary; four minutes means whatever it is waiting for is not answering.

choices.text: Look underneath: the device it is waiting on
choices.why: Right — `D` is a symptom, and the cause is the device that is not answering.

prompt: You find a `Z` process. `kill -9` does nothing to it. Why not?
hint: Ask what is left of it to receive anything.

choices.text: It is over; there is nothing left to receive it
choices.why: Right — what remains is a table entry holding a number nobody has read.

choices.text: It is a protected process, the way PID 1 is
choices.why: No process is protected from `KILL` by the kernel; permission is the only check.

choices.text: It is blocking signals with a trap
choices.why: `KILL` cannot be trapped by anything, and a finished process runs no code.

choices.text: It is in uninterruptible sleep inside a call to the kernel
choices.why: That is `D`; a zombie is not sleeping, it has finished.

prompt: Thousands of zombies have accumulated. What is the actual damage, and what fixes it?
hint: A zombie holds one thing, and it is not memory.

choices.text: They hold memory; reboot to reclaim it
choices.why: A zombie holds no memory, no files and no processor; that is what makes it a zombie.

choices.text: They fill the process table; fix the parent
choices.why: Right — and when the buggy parent exits, PID 1 collects its zombies at once.

choices.text: They spin; renice the parent
choices.why: A finished process is not scheduled at all and uses no processor.

choices.text: They keep their files open
choices.why: Everything a zombie had open was released when it exited.

prompt: Match each `STAT` letter to what it means.
hint: Five letters, five different reasons a process is not using the processor right now — or is.

pairs.right: running, or queued to run
asleep, and a signal would wake it
asleep on the kernel, and no signal will
suspended, holding everything it had
finished, status not yet collected

right_distractors: waiting for a lock held by root

prompt: `ps` writes ____ in place of a command line for a zombie, because there is no program left to name.
hint: Nine letters, and `ps` puts it in square brackets.

prompt: You want to know which account started what. Which of these two, and why?
hint: One of the two carries a parent column and the other carries resource columns.

choices.text: `ps aux`, because it has the `USER` column
choices.why: Both print a user; the question is the parent, and `aux` leaves that out.

choices.text: `ps -ef`, because it prints `PPID` as well
choices.why: Right — `-ef` is the who-started-what listing and `aux` is the resource one.

choices.text: `ps aux`, because `-ef` hides processes owned by other accounts
choices.why: Both list every process on the machine; neither hides anything by account.

choices.text: `ps -ef`, because `aux` is the older BSD spelling and is deprecated
choices.why: Both are current and neither is going away; they differ in columns, not in age.

prompt: A process shows `VSZ` of 2.1 GB and `RSS` of 40 MB. How much memory is it using?
hint: One column counts what was mapped and the other what was touched.

choices.text: 2.1 GB, with RSS swapped in
choices.why: Swap has its own accounting; RSS is what is resident regardless of what swap is doing.

choices.text: Somewhere between the two, and no column says
choices.why: One of them answers it directly, and it is the smaller one.

choices.text: 40 MB virtual, 2.1 GB reserved
choices.why: Nothing is reserved on disk by mapping; the terms are the wrong way round here.

choices.text: About 40 MB — `RSS` is what is in physical memory
choices.why: Right, and `VSZ` includes everything mapped and never touched.

prompt: `%CPU` in `ps` says 92 for a process that `top` shows at 0. Which is lying?
hint: The two columns are measured over different windows.

choices.text: Neither: `ps` averages over the whole life and `top` samples now
choices.why: Right — a process that pinned a core for an hour and then stopped shows exactly this.

choices.text: `top`, because batch mode's first sample reads zero
choices.why: That is true of `top -b -n 1` and would not explain a 92 in `ps`.

choices.text: `ps`, because it counts the time of children that have exited
choices.why: That needs `cputime` accounting to be asked for; the plain column is this process.

choices.text: `top`, because it divides by the number of processors and `ps` does not
choices.why: Both express `%CPU` per processor; the header line is the one that divides.

prompt: Why does `pgrep -f sleeper.sh` find the script when `pgrep sleeper.sh` does not?
hint: Think about what the program's name actually is when you run a shell script.

choices.text: `-f` follows symlinks
choices.why: `-f` has nothing to do with links; it changes what text is matched.

choices.text: `-f` forces a match
choices.why: Several matches are fine without it; `pgrep` prints one PID per line.

choices.text: Without `-f` it matches the program name, which is `bash`
choices.why: Right — the script is an argument, so only the full command line contains its name.

choices.text: Without `-f` it is limited to processes owned by root
choices.why: Ownership is `-u`, and by default `pgrep` looks at every account.

prompt: `ps aux | grep nginx` prints one row and nginx is not running. What happened?
hint: Look at the command line of the thing that matched.

choices.text: `ps` matched its own row, which contains the whole nginx pipeline
choices.why: `ps` snapshots before the pipe is read and does not list the whole pipeline as one row.

choices.text: `grep` matched itself, as its own arguments contain the word
choices.why: Right, and `grep -v grep` is the usual patch on top of it.

choices.text: A cached entry from the last time nginx ran is still in `/proc`
choices.why: `/proc` has no cache; a directory disappears the moment the process does.

choices.text: The shell expanded `nginx` from history before `ps` ran
choices.why: History expansion needs a `!`, and it would have rewritten the line you see.

prompt: Complete the single most useful `ps`, sorted so the heaviest process comes first: `ps -eo pid,comm,%cpu --sort=____ | head`
hint: The column name with a sign in front of it to reverse the order.

prompt: A script started three background children. You kill the script by its PID. What happens to the children?
hint: A signal reaches one process, and the kernel has a rule for what is left over.

choices.text: They are killed with it, since they belong to the script
choices.why: Belonging does not propagate a signal; each child is its own process.

choices.text: They are suspended until something adopts them
choices.why: Nothing suspends them; they carry on at full speed while their parent slot is empty.

choices.text: They keep running, and their PPID becomes 1
choices.why: Right — the kernel re-parents an orphan to process one, which collects it later.

choices.text: They are killed, because a process with no parent is removed
choices.why: A process with no parent is given one; that is exactly what adoption is.

prompt: In `pstree` output, `10*[{process_api}]` means what?
hint: The braces and the star are two separate notations, and both are in that one entry.

choices.text: Ten processes named `process_api`
choices.why: The braces mark threads, and `ps` shows all ten as one row rather than ten.

choices.text: A process restarted ten times
choices.why: `pstree` does not track restarts; it draws what exists right now.

choices.text: Ten child processes whose names `pstree` could not read
choices.why: An unreadable name would not be repeated ten times with a count in front of it.

choices.text: One process with ten threads, collapsed into a single entry
choices.why: Right — the star is the count and the braces mean thread rather than process.

prompt: Something unexpected is running and you want to know what started it. One command.
hint: You have its number; you want the chain above it.

choices.text: `pstree -s PID`
choices.why: Right — it prints the chain from that process up to PID 1 in one line.

choices.text: `pstree -p PID`
choices.why: That draws what is below it, which is the opposite direction.

choices.text: `pstree -u PID`
choices.why: `-u` marks where the account changes; on its own it does not climb.

choices.text: `pstree -n PID`
choices.why: `-n` sorts by PID instead of by name, and still draws downward.

prompt: `ps -ef | awk '$3==1'` lists processes whose parent is gone. The column it is testing is called ____.
hint: Four letters, and it is the column right after PID.

prompt: `top` shows one process at `100.0` and the header line at `25.0 us`. The machine has four processors. Who is right?
hint: The two numbers have different denominators.

choices.text: The header; the process column counts threads, so it overstates the machine
choices.why: The process column is per process, and threads only appear with `-H`.

choices.text: Both: one is per processor, the other per machine
choices.why: Right — one saturated core out of four is 100 in one column and 25 in the other.

choices.text: The process column; the header averages over the last minute and lags
choices.why: The load average lags; the `%Cpu(s)` line is a sample of the interval just passed.

choices.text: Neither, because batch mode measures one frame
choices.why: A single frame is measured against the process's whole life, which is a different caveat.

prompt: `load average: 8.10, 8.05, 7.98` on a machine with eight processors. What does it tell you?
hint: Compare the number to something, and read the three positions as a shape.

choices.text: A spike that started in the last minute and will pass
choices.why: A spike shows a high first number and lower later ones; these three barely differ.

choices.text: Eight processes are stuck in uninterruptible sleep
choices.why: `D` counts towards load, but nothing here says the load is made of it.

choices.text: The processors are 8% busy, which is comfortable
choices.why: Load is a count of what wanted to run, not a percentage of anything.

choices.text: Saturated, and steady for a quarter of an hour
choices.why: Right — 8 on eight processors is saturated, and the flat trio means sustained.

prompt: A machine reports `0.5 us`, `0.3 sy`, `60.0 wa` and a load of 30. What is wrong with it?
hint: Read which column is large, then ask what that column counts.

choices.text: The processors are completely saturated and the load confirms it
choices.why: The processors are 99% idle; the `us` and `sy` columns are near zero.

choices.text: Thirty processes are spinning in a busy loop somewhere
choices.why: A busy loop shows up as `us`, and that column is at half a percent.

choices.text: Storage is behind, and the load is the queue for it
choices.why: Right — `wa` is I/O wait, and load counts `D` as well as `R`.

choices.text: A hypervisor is taking the machine's time away from it
choices.why: That is the `st` column, which is not the one that is large here.

prompt: `free -h` reports 561 MiB used, 14 GiB free, 892 MiB buff/cache and 15 GiB available. Which number answers 'can I start something big'?
hint: One of the four is computed for exactly this question.

choices.text: `available`, at 15 GiB
choices.why: Right — it counts the cache as reclaimable, which is what the kernel treats it as.

choices.text: `free`, at 14 GiB, with cache in use
choices.why: Cache is handed back the moment a program asks, so counting it as used is pessimistic.

choices.text: `used` subtracted, about 15.4 GiB
choices.why: That ignores the kernel's own overhead, which `available` accounts for.

choices.text: `buff/cache`, at 892 MiB
choices.why: That is one input to the answer rather than the answer itself.

prompt: Match each `%Cpu(s)` abbreviation to what it counts.
hint: Four of the eight, and two of them point at something outside the machine's own programs.

pairs.right: your programs, doing their own work
the kernel, working on their behalf
time lost waiting for storage
time a hypervisor gave to somebody else

prompt: Show every processor on its own line in interactive `top` by pressing ____.
hint: A single digit.

prompt: Which two signals cannot be caught, blocked or ignored?
hint: One removes the process and one freezes it, and the kernel handles both itself.

choices.text: `TERM` and `INT`
choices.why: Both of those are routinely caught; that is how a program cleans up before leaving.

choices.text: `HUP` and `TERM`
choices.why: `HUP` is caught constantly, which is how daemons use it to reload.

choices.text: `KILL` and `QUIT`
choices.why: `QUIT` can be caught; it just writes a core dump by default.

choices.text: `KILL` and `STOP`
choices.why: Right — a program that could refuse either would be one you could not manage.

prompt: A background job finished with `[1]+ Killed` and its `trap` printed nothing. Which signal did it get?
hint: The trap is still in the script. Something did not consult it.

choices.text: `TERM`, and the trap had a bug
choices.why: A `TERM` trap that runs prints something; silence is the evidence it never ran.

choices.text: `HUP`, the terminal went
choices.why: A hangup reports as `Hangup` rather than `Killed`, and it can be trapped.

choices.text: `KILL`, which has no handler
choices.why: Right — `Killed` and a silent trap together are the signature of `kill -9`.

choices.text: `STOP`, suspended first
choices.why: A stopped job reports `Stopped` and is still there afterwards.

prompt: `yes | head -2` ends, and `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is 141. What does 141 mean?
hint: It is above 128, which is a hint about how it is built.

choices.text: `yes` was killed by signal 13, which is `SIGPIPE`
choices.why: Right — 128 plus the signal number, and `head` had already closed the pipe.

choices.text: `yes` chose to exit with 141 to report a write error
choices.why: `yes` has no such convention; the number came from how it died, not from a choice.

choices.text: 141 bytes were written before the pipe closed on it
choices.why: An exit status is a status, not a byte count.

choices.text: The shell returned 141 because the pipeline had an unhandled stage
choices.why: Bash reports the last stage's status, and `head` exited cleanly with 0.

prompt: `kill -0 PID` returns 1 for two very different situations. Which two, and why does it matter?
hint: Read the two messages bash prints; then read the exit status of each.

choices.text: Signal blocked, or process stopped — and a stopped one needs `CONT` first
choices.why: Blocking does not fail the call, and a stopped process accepts signals normally.

choices.text: Gone, or not yours — and `$?` alone cannot tell them apart
choices.why: Right, and the two call for opposite responses, so the message is the part that matters.

choices.text: Zombie, or kernel thread — neither can be signalled
choices.why: A zombie and a kernel thread both pass the existence check that `-0` performs.

choices.text: Bad PID syntax, or a PID above the wrap limit — both are argument errors
choices.why: Those are usage errors and report differently from a refused or missing process.

prompt: Match each signal to what sends it or what it is for.
hint: Six of the sixty-four, and each one has a distinct occasion.

pairs.right: the Ctrl+C key
the polite stop, and kill's default
removal, with no chance to clean up
the terminal went away, or reload me
a child of yours has exited
the program touched memory it does not own

right_distractors: a timer you set has expired

prompt: Catch `SIGTERM` in a bash script and run `cleanup` when it arrives: `____ cleanup TERM`
hint: Four letters, and it is a shell builtin.

prompt: `kill 2189` on a root-owned process fails. Does `kill -9 2189` get through?
hint: Work out at what point the refusal happens.

choices.text: Yes, because `-9` is handled by the kernel rather than the process
choices.why: The kernel handles the signal and also performs the permission check, in that order.

choices.text: Yes, for processes that share your own session
choices.why: Sessions do not grant signalling rights; the account does.

choices.text: No — the permission check runs before any signal is chosen
choices.why: Right, so `-9` fails in exactly the way the polite one did.

choices.text: No, but `-9` succeeds once the process stops holding a lock
choices.why: Locks have nothing to do with it; the refusal is about ownership.

prompt: A script started three children. `kill $PID` on the script leaves the children running; `kill %1` does not. What is the difference?
hint: One of them names a process and the other names something bigger.

choices.text: `%1` sends `KILL` while a bare `kill` sends `TERM`
choices.why: Both default to `TERM`; the difference is who receives it, not which signal.

choices.text: `%1` names the job's process group, so all of it is signalled
choices.why: Right — bash made the group when it started the command, and `%1` refers to the group.

choices.text: `%1` waits for the children to finish before killing the parent
choices.why: It waits for nothing; the whole group is signalled at once.

choices.text: `%1` re-parents the children to the shell first, and then kills all of them
choices.why: Orphans go to PID 1, and nothing re-parents anything to a shell.

prompt: Why is `kill -- -2684` written with two dashes in front of the group number?
hint: Ask what bash would make of the number if the dashes were not there.

choices.text: `--` tells `kill` to signal the group rather than the leader
choices.why: The minus sign in front of the number does that; `--` is about option parsing.

choices.text: `--` suppresses the error message when part of the group is gone
choices.why: Nothing is suppressed; the call reports whether it signalled anything.

choices.text: `--` is needed for a variable
choices.why: Variables need no such marker; the problem is the leading minus sign.

choices.text: Without it, `-2684` is read as a signal number
choices.why: Right — bash answers with `invalid signal specification`.

prompt: `pkill -f watcher` also killed a `tail -f watcher.log` that had nothing to do with it. What is the habit that prevents this?
hint: The two commands take the same options for a reason.

choices.text: Run the match through `pgrep` first and read the list
choices.why: Right — `pgrep` prints what `pkill` would signal, with identical options.

choices.text: Use `pkill -x` so the pattern has to match the whole line
choices.why: `-x` requires an exact match of the name, which would then miss the script too.

choices.text: Add `-u` so the match is limited to your own account
choices.why: Both processes here belong to the same account, so that changes nothing.

choices.text: Use `killall` instead, which matches the program name
choices.why: That helps for this pair and misses scripts entirely, since the program is `bash`.

prompt: Put the steps of stopping a process that is not responding in order.
items: kill -0 PID to see whether it is still there
trap: Ask politely, give it time, check, and only then remove it.

prompt: Which of these are real consequences of `kill -9` on a database?
hint: The trap never runs. Work forward from there.

choices.text: It cannot flush what it was holding, so the next start is a recovery
choices.why: Yes — the shutdown code it would have run is the code that flushes.

choices.text: A lock or PID file is left behind and the next start refuses
choices.why: Yes, and that is the most common visible symptom the next morning.

choices.text: Its children are left running, because it never got to stop them
choices.why: Yes — a signal to one process is a signal to one process.

choices.text: Its files are corrupted at the filesystem level and need fsck
choices.why: The filesystem is consistent; what is inconsistent is the application's own data.

choices.text: The kernel refuses if the process holds a lock another process wants
choices.why: Nothing checks locks; `KILL` is not refusable on those grounds.

prompt: Ask `killall` to name each process it stops, so you can see what you hit: `killall ____ watcher.sh`
hint: One short flag.

prompt: You pressed `Ctrl+Z` on a download an hour ago. How much has it downloaded since?
hint: Look up what state `Ctrl+Z` leaves a process in.

choices.text: All of it, since suspending only detaches it from the keyboard
choices.why: Detaching from the keyboard is what `bg` does; `Ctrl+Z` stops the process.

choices.text: Whatever fits in the buffer
choices.why: The buffer fills in moments, so the honest answer rounds to the same as none.

choices.text: About as much as an hour of running, minus scheduling overhead
choices.why: A stopped process is not scheduled at all, so it gets no processor and no progress.

choices.text: None — a stopped process is suspended, not backgrounded
choices.why: Right, and `bg` is what you needed; `Ctrl+Z` on its own just parks it.

prompt: You started a long command in the foreground and want your prompt back without losing it. Which two steps?
hint: Two keystrokes and then two letters.

choices.text: `Ctrl+Z`, then `bg`
choices.why: Right — stop it, then resume it without the terminal.

choices.text: `Ctrl+Z`, then `fg`
choices.why: `fg` resumes it in the foreground, which puts you back where you started.

choices.text: `Ctrl+C`, then run it again with `&`
choices.why: That throws away whatever it had done and starts over.

choices.text: `Ctrl+Z`, then `disown`
choices.why: `disown` forgets the job while it is still stopped, so it stays stopped forever.

prompt: `Ctrl+D` at a shell prompt closes the shell. Which signal does it send?
hint: It does not belong in the same list as the other two keys.

choices.text: `SIGHUP`, the very signal a closed terminal sends to a shell
choices.why: A closed terminal sends that; the key does something else entirely.

choices.text: `SIGQUIT`, which is why no message is printed
choices.why: `SIGQUIT` is `Ctrl+\`, and it writes a core dump rather than exiting quietly.

choices.text: None — it is end of input, and reading it ends bash
choices.why: Right, which is why it does nothing at all to a program that is not reading.

choices.text: `SIGINT`, delivered to the foreground process group
choices.why: That is `Ctrl+C`, and at a prompt it gives you a new line rather than an exit.

prompt: After `disown %1`, `jobs` is empty and `ps` still shows the process with the shell as its parent. What did `disown` change?
hint: One of those two commands reads the shell's own memory and the other reads the kernel's.

choices.text: It detached the process from the terminal, which is why `jobs` is empty
choices.why: The terminal is unchanged; a disowned job still writes to your screen.

choices.text: The shell's bookkeeping, so it will not send the job a hangup on exit
choices.why: Right — the process is untouched, and what changed is what bash will do later.

choices.text: The process's parent, which is now PID 1
choices.why: `ps` in the question shows the shell still as the parent; nothing was re-parented.

choices.text: The job's process group, so the shell no longer signals it as a group
choices.why: The group is the kernel's and is unchanged; bash simply stopped tracking the job.

prompt: Show the job list with each job's PID next to it: `jobs ____`
hint: One short flag.

prompt: Three identical background jobs; after the terminal closed, only the plain one died. Why did the other two survive?
hint: One was told to ignore the signal and the other was never sent it.

choices.text: Both were re-parented to PID 1 well before the signal was ever delivered
choices.why: Adoption happens after the parent exits, which is after the signal goes out.

choices.text: Both had their output redirected, so the hangup could not reach them
choices.why: Redirection changes where writes go and nothing about signal delivery.

choices.text: `nohup` ignored the signal; the disowned one was never sent it
choices.why: Right — two different mechanisms with the same outcome.

choices.text: Both were started with `&`, which detaches a job from its session
choices.why: `&` backgrounds a job and leaves it in the same session; all three used it.

prompt: A four-hour job is already running in the foreground and you have to close your laptop. What do you reach for?
hint: It is already started, so one of the two is no longer available to you.

choices.text: `Ctrl+Z`, `bg`, then `disown`
choices.why: Right — `nohup` had to be decided beforehand, and `disown` is the rescue.

choices.text: `nohup` on the running process
choices.why: `nohup` wraps a command you are about to start; it cannot be applied afterwards.

choices.text: `setsid` on the running process
choices.why: `setsid` also starts something new; it does not move a running process into a session.

choices.text: `systemctl` to adopt it
choices.why: systemd starts services from unit files rather than adopting a process you already have.

prompt: The job must survive a reboot, restart if it crashes, and be findable by a colleague. Which of these?
hint: Three requirements, and only one of the options meets the first two.

choices.text: `nohup` with a log file
choices.why: It survives a closed terminal and not a reboot, and it restarts nothing.

choices.text: `setsid`, no terminal
choices.why: Same limitation: detached is not the same as supervised.

choices.text: A `tmux` session left open
choices.why: A reboot takes tmux with it, and nothing restarts the job afterwards.

choices.text: A unit file for systemd
choices.why: Right — boot, restart and a name a colleague can look up are what a unit is for.

prompt: Name the file `nohup` writes output to when you do not redirect it yourself: ____
hint: Two words joined by a dot, in the current directory.

prompt: Which nice value makes a process step aside for everything else?
hint: The name is the right way round: a nice process is a polite one.

choices.why: That end is the demanding one, and only root can ask for it.
Right — the highest value is the most polite, and it runs when nothing else wants to.
Zero is the default every process already has, so it yields to nothing in particular.
The range stops at 19; a larger number is clamped.

prompt: You set a process to nice 15, then try `renice -n 5` on it. It is your own process. What happens?
hint: Niceness moves freely in one direction for an unprivileged account.

choices.text: It works without complaint, since you own the process yourself
choices.why: Ownership lets you raise the value; it does not let you lower it again.

choices.text: It works, until it next sleeps
choices.why: Niceness does not reset when a process sleeps; it is a property of the process.

choices.text: `Permission denied` — it ratchets upward
choices.why: Right, and the account that set it in the first place is refused along with everybody else.

choices.text: It works and the scheduler quietly clamps it back to 15
choices.why: Nothing is clamped silently; `renice` reports what it refused.

prompt: Two identical busy loops share one pinned processor for thirty seconds, at nice 0 and nice 19. What do their CPU times look like?
hint: Ask what a nice value of 19 means when there is competition.

choices.text: About thirty seconds and about nothing
choices.why: Right — 19 means run when nobody else wants to, and somebody else did the whole time.

choices.text: About fifteen seconds each, since both were runnable throughout
choices.why: Equal shares are what you get at equal niceness; the point of 19 is that it is not equal.

choices.text: About twenty and about ten
choices.why: Niceness is not a ratio of the numbers; the weighting is far steeper than that.

choices.text: About thirty seconds each, because niceness applies per processor
choices.why: Both were pinned to the same processor, so thirty seconds is all there was to share.

prompt: A nightly backup is making the database slow, and `top` shows the backup using almost no processor. Which knob helps?
hint: Find out which resource is actually contended before choosing a tool.

choices.text: `renice -n 19` on the backup
choices.why: Niceness is processor time, and the backup is barely asking for any.

choices.text: `renice -n -5` on the database
choices.why: It is not a processor contest, and negative values need root as well.

choices.text: `kill -STOP` on the backup
choices.why: That holds the backup's locks and files open, which makes it a diagnostic rather than a plan.

choices.text: `ionice -c 3` on the backup
choices.why: Right — the contention is the disk, and idle-class I/O is the matching knob.

prompt: `nice -n -5 true` as an ordinary user prints `Permission denied` and `$?` is 0. Why is that a trap?
hint: Read what the exit status is describing.

choices.text: The status is the shell's, and `nice` did not get to run
choices.why: `nice` ran and printed the refusal; what it could not do was change the value.

choices.text: `nice` ran the command anyway, so the status is the command's
choices.why: Right — a script checking `$?` learns nothing about whether the niceness was applied.

choices.text: `nice` retried at a value it was allowed, so the status reports success
choices.why: It does not retry; it keeps the niceness it already had and carries on.

choices.text: `true` overwrote a non-zero status that `nice` had set
choices.why: `nice` does not set a status of its own when it goes on to run the command.

prompt: Start a reindex at the most polite priority there is: `____ -n 19 ./nightly-reindex.sh`
hint: Four letters.

prompt: What does `2>&1` actually ask for?
hint: Both numbers name entries in one table.

choices.text: Send errors to a file called `&1`
choices.why: The ampersand is what stops it meaning a file; without it that is exactly what happens.

choices.text: Run the command twice, once per stream
choices.why: Nothing is run twice; redirection is set up before the program starts.

choices.text: Make descriptor 2 a copy of descriptor 1
choices.why: Right — errors go wherever output is currently going.

choices.text: Merge the two streams into a new descriptor numbered 3
choices.why: No new descriptor appears; 2 is pointed at what 1 already refers to.

prompt: A log file was deleted, `du` finds nothing large, and `df` still reports the disk full. What is happening?
hint: Lesson 3 said `rm` removes a name.

choices.text: The filesystem needs `fsck` to release the blocks
choices.why: The filesystem is consistent; nothing is waiting to be repaired.

choices.text: `du` is reading a stale cache and needs the directory re-scanned
choices.why: `du` walks the tree afresh each time; it has no cache to go stale.

choices.text: The blocks are reserved for root and `df` counts them as used
choices.why: Root reserve is a fixed fraction and does not change when a file is deleted.

choices.text: Something holds it open, so the blocks stay allocated
choices.why: Right — `lsof +L1` finds it, and the fix is to restart or `HUP` that process.

prompt: A service logs `Too many open files`. Which limit has it hit, and what usually causes it?
hint: Network connections live in the same table as files.

choices.text: `ulimit -n`, and the cause is opening without closing
choices.why: Right, and `ls -l /proc/PID/fd` normally names the repeated culprit.

choices.text: `ulimit -u`, the process count
choices.why: Opening a file forks nothing; `-u` counts processes.

choices.text: The inode limit of the filesystem, which can count open files too
choices.why: Inodes are a filesystem property and are unrelated to how many a process has open.

choices.text: `ulimit -f`, the maximum file size, reached across many files at once
choices.why: `-f` limits how large one file may grow, not how many there are.

prompt: Match each descriptor number to what it is by convention.
hint: Three numbers every program is handed before it starts.

pairs.right: standard input
standard output
standard error

prompt: List every open file that no longer has a name, in one command: `lsof ____`
hint: A plus sign, a letter and a digit.

prompt: A cron job's log ends with status 127. What went wrong?
hint: It is one of two numbers about the command itself rather than its work.

choices.text: It reported 127 failures
choices.why: A count would be the program's own choice; 127 is reserved for something else.

choices.text: The command was not found
choices.why: Right — a typo, or a program that is not installed where cron looked.

choices.text: Killed by signal 127
choices.why: Signals add to 128, so a killed process reports above it rather than below.

choices.text: The command timed out after 127 seconds of running
choices.why: Timeouts report their own status, and nothing encodes a duration in one.

prompt: A container keeps restarting and its last status is 137. What killed it?
hint: Subtract 128 and look the remainder up.

choices.text: The application, which chose 137 as its own error code
choices.why: 137 above 128 is the kernel's arithmetic rather than a program's choice.

choices.text: The health check, after failures
choices.why: A probe failure does not put its count into an exit status.

choices.text: A `SIGTERM`, as can happen during a rolling restart
choices.why: `TERM` is 15, which gives 143 rather than 137.

choices.text: `SIGKILL` — most often the out-of-memory killer
choices.why: Right: 128 plus 9, and nothing polite sends `KILL` on its own.

prompt: `curl https://example.test/x | tar xz` and `$?` is 0, but nothing was extracted. Why did the status not say so?
hint: Which stage does a pipeline's status come from?

choices.text: `$?` is the last stage only, so `curl` failing is invisible
choices.why: Right — and `set -o pipefail` or `PIPESTATUS` is how you see the earlier stage.

choices.text: `tar` swallows errors from standard input and always exits 0
choices.why: `tar` reports its own problems; the issue is which status the shell kept.

choices.text: `curl` exits 0 on an HTTP error unless `-f` is given
choices.why: That is a real `curl` wart and a different one: here the shell discarded the status.

choices.text: The pipe returns the status of whichever stage failed first
choices.why: That is what `pipefail` makes it do; the default is the last stage.

prompt: `grep pattern file` returns 1 in a script running under `set -e`, and the script stops. Is that a bug?
hint: Ask what `grep`'s 1 means before asking what `set -e` should do about it.

choices.text: Yes — 1 should be ignored
choices.why: `set -e` treats every non-zero status the same way; there is no threshold.

choices.text: No — a status of 1 from `grep` can mean the file could not be read
choices.why: An unreadable file is 2; 1 is a clean search that matched nothing.

choices.text: Yes in effect: 1 means no match, a perfectly normal answer
choices.why: Right — put it in an `if`, or append `|| true` when you expect no match.

choices.text: No — `set -e` does not act on the last command of a pipeline anyway
choices.why: It acts on it; the exemptions are conditions and commands joined by `&&` or `||`.

prompt: Match each exit status to what produced it.
hint: Five numbers, and two of them are about the command rather than its work.

pairs.right: it worked
grep found no match
found the file, could not execute it
no such command
somebody pressed Ctrl+C

right_distractors: the argument was out of range

prompt: Make a pipeline report the last non-zero status instead of the last stage's: `set -o ____`
hint: One word, eight letters.

prompt: A machine is slow. `top` shows `%Cpu(s): 3.0 us, 1.0 sy, 0.0 wa, 96.0 id` and a load average of 0.4. Where do you look next?
hint: Every column you have been given is small. That is itself the finding.

choices.text: At the process list sorted by `%CPU`, for the runaway
choices.why: There is nothing to find: 96% idle and a load under one means nothing is queuing.

choices.text: At `ps` for processes in `D`, since the load is hiding them
choices.why: Processes in `D` push the load up, and this load is low.

choices.text: Somewhere other than the processor — memory, network or the application
choices.why: Right — this machine is not busy, so the slowness is not a scheduling problem.

choices.text: At the load average over a longer window, since one minute is too short
choices.why: All three figures are available in the same line, and none of them is high.

prompt: Put these in the order you would work through an unfamiliar process that is eating the machine.
trap: Find it, find out what started it, find out what it is, ask it to stop, and only then remove it.

prompt: A service was stopped an hour ago and its port is still in use. `ps` shows no process by that name. What is the most likely explanation?
hint: Killing a parent leaves something behind, and it was covered twice in this lesson.

choices.text: The kernel holds the port for an hour after the last close
choices.why: A closed socket does linger, and in seconds rather than an hour.

choices.text: A child of the service is still running, adopted by PID 1
choices.why: Right — `ss -lptn` names the process, and its `PPID` will be `1`.

choices.text: The service left a zombie that still owns the socket
choices.why: A zombie holds no files and no sockets; everything was released when it exited.

choices.text: The port is bound by a systemd socket unit rather than the service
choices.why: That is a real arrangement and it would be listed under systemd rather than missing.

prompt: You have a PID and want three things: what it is, what started it, and whether it is yours to signal. Which three commands?
hint: One reads `/proc`, one climbs, and one asks without sending anything.

choices.text: `ls -l /proc/PID/exe`, `pstree -s PID`, `kill -0 PID`
choices.why: Right — the binary, the ancestry, and the permission check that sends nothing.

choices.text: `ps -p PID`, `ps -ef | grep PID`, `kill -9 PID`
choices.why: The last one answers the question by acting on it, which is not the same as asking.

choices.text: `lsof -p PID`, `pstree -p PID`, `renice -n 0 -p PID`
choices.why: `pstree -p` looks downward, and `renice` changes the process to find out about it.

choices.text: `cat /proc/PID/status`, `pgrep -P PID`, `killall -0 PID`
choices.why: `pgrep -P` lists children, and `killall` takes a name rather than a number.

prompt: Which of these leave a process running after you close the terminal?
hint: Two mechanisms work, one is about the shell's list, and two do nothing for this.

choices.text: `nohup cmd &`
choices.why: Yes — the signal arrives and is ignored.

choices.text: `cmd &` followed by `disown`
choices.why: Yes — bash forgets the job and never sends the signal.

choices.text: `setsid cmd &`
choices.why: Yes — there is no controlling terminal to hang up in the first place.

choices.text: `cmd &` on its own
choices.why: No — this is the one that died in the experiment.

choices.text: `cmd &` with `renice -n 19`
choices.why: Niceness is scheduling; it has nothing to do with hangups.

prompt: A colleague says the machine has 400 processes because `top` said `Tasks: 400`. What would you check?
hint: Two of this lesson's sections warned about this same count.

choices.text: `ps -e | wc -l`, since `top` counts kernel threads and `ps` does not
choices.why: Both include kernel threads; neither hides them.

choices.text: The load average, which counts the same things `Tasks:` does
choices.why: Load counts what wanted to run, not what exists.

choices.text: `/proc`, since `top` includes directories left by exited processes
choices.why: A `/proc` entry disappears with its process; nothing is left behind.

choices.text: Whether `-H` is on, since that counts threads rather than processes
choices.why: Right — the header says `Threads:` instead of `Tasks:` when it is.

prompt: Match each symptom to the thing to reach for first.
hint: Six symptoms from across the lesson, each with one first move.

pairs.left: one process at 100% on a four-core box
pairs.right: renice it, then find out why
look at storage and the wa column
fix the parent that is not reaping

pairs.left: disk full and du finds nothing
pairs.right: lsof +L1 for a deleted open file

pairs.left: Too many open files in a log
pairs.right: count /proc/PID/fd and raise LimitNOFILE

pairs.left: a job died when the laptop closed
pairs.right: nohup or disown, next time

right_distractors: clear the page cache by hand

prompt: One line that answers "what is eating this machine": `ps -eo pid,comm,%cpu --sort=-%cpu | ____`
hint: Four letters, and it keeps the first few lines.

prompt: Put the life of a backgrounded command in order, from the shell to the orphan.
items: bash forks a copy of itself
the copy execs the program you named
bash prints [1] and the PID, and does not wait
you close the terminal and bash sends SIGHUP
the job is gone, or survives with PPID 1
trap: Copy, replace, skip the wait, and then the terminal goes away.

prompt: Which pair of states means the same thing to the processor — no instructions being run?
hint: Four of the five states are not on a processor at all.

choices.text: `R` and `S`
choices.why: `R` is exactly the one that is on or waiting for a processor.

choices.text: `R` and `Z`
choices.why: `R` is doing work by definition; the zombie is the one that is not.

choices.text: `T` and `Z`
choices.why: Right — stopped and finished, and neither is given any processor time.

choices.text: `D` and `R`
choices.why: `D` is asleep in the kernel and `R` is runnable; only one of them gets a processor.

prompt: Which of these actually reduces the time a process spends waiting on a busy disk?
hint: Three of the four are about the processor.

choices.text: `renice -n 19` on the process
choices.why: Niceness is processor time, and a process waiting on a disk is asking for none.

choices.text: `taskset -c 0` to pin it
choices.why: Pinning changes which processor it uses, not how the disk is shared.

choices.text: `kill -STOP` and `kill -CONT` in turn
choices.why: That pauses the process entirely and holds its open files while it waits.

choices.text: `ionice -c 3` on the process
choices.why: Right — idle-class I/O is the knob for disk contention.

prompt: You need a deploy script to stop a service the way `systemctl stop` would. What does it have to do?
hint: Lesson 5 described the sequence; this lesson supplied every piece of it.

choices.text: `kill -9` the main PID, and then delete its PID file by hand
choices.why: That is the sequence `systemctl stop` exists to avoid.

choices.text: `TERM` the group, wait, then `KILL` what is left
choices.why: Right — polite first, a deadline, and removal only for what ignored it.

choices.text: `TERM` the main PID alone
choices.why: `kill` returns as soon as the signal is queued, which says nothing about the children.

choices.text: `STOP` the group, check that it is quiet, then `KILL` it
choices.why: A stopped process keeps its locks and files, so this makes the cleanup worse.

prompt: `ps` reports `%CPU` of 0.0 for a process you can see is busy. Which command would show the truth?
hint: One column is a lifetime average and the other is a sample.

choices.text: `top -b -n 2 -d 1`, whose second frame is an interval
choices.why: Right — two frames a second apart give `top` something to measure between.

choices.text: `ps -eo pid,%cpu --sort=-%cpu`, which recomputes the column
choices.why: It is the same lifetime average, sorted; sorting does not change what it measures.

choices.text: `pstree -p`, which shows live activity per branch
choices.why: `pstree` draws structure and reports no activity at all.

choices.text: `/proc/PID/status`, which holds the current figure
choices.why: It holds counters and state; the rate has to be computed from two readings.

prompt: Resume a stopped job in the background, in two letters: `____`
hint: It is the opposite of `fg`.

prompt: Complete the check that asks whether a process exists and is yours, without sending it anything: `kill ____ $PID`
hint: A dash and a digit.
